title: Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in association with exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease: a case report
case_prompt:
A 55-year-old woman with a 5-year history of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, poorly compliant with inhaler therapy and a 30-pack-year smoking history, was transferred after developing multiple seizures followed by loss of consciousness on the first day of treatment for acute COPD exacerbation. Family history was unremarkable. 

On arrival she was drowsy and not following commands. Temperature was 37.6 °C, blood pressure 130/80 mmHg, pulse 96/min, and respiratory rate 26/min. Lung examination revealed widespread expiratory wheezes. As she regained consciousness, she complained of headache and decreased vision. Ocular examination showed normally reactive pupils and a normal fundus; cranial nerves, motor, and sensory examinations were otherwise unremarkable. There were no signs of meningeal irritation.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 17 g/dL, white-cell count 12 640/µL, platelets 155 000/µL, urea 37 mg/dL, creatinine 0.3 mg/dL, sodium 132 meq/L, and potassium 4.6 meq/L. Chest radiography demonstrated emphysematous changes. Arterial blood gas analysis revealed pH 7.56, pCO2 46.2 mmHg, pO2 81.0 mmHg, and HCO3– 41.5 mmol/L. 

Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain (T2 and FLAIR sequences) showed diffuse confluent white-matter hyperintensities in the bilateral parieto-occipital regions.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stroke was considered because of acute neurologic symptoms but was excluded by the absence of focal diffusion-restricted lesions and the presence of bilateral posterior vasogenic edema — “Typical MRI findings in PRES are of bilateral white-matter abnormalities in vascular watershed areas in the posterior regions of both cerebral hemispheres, affecting mostly the occipital and parietal lobes.”  
2. Cerebral venous thrombosis was considered in the setting of headache and seizures but was excluded by the lack of venous sinus abnormalities and by the characteristic bilateral parieto-occipital hyperintensities — “Typical MRI findings in PRES are of bilateral white-matter abnormalities in vascular watershed areas in the posterior regions of both cerebral hemispheres, affecting mostly the occipital and parietal lobes.”  
3. Toxic or metabolic encephalopathy was considered due to altered mental status but was excluded by the focal pattern of white-matter edema rather than diffuse cortical involvement — “Typical MRI findings in PRES are of bilateral white-matter abnormalities in vascular watershed areas in the posterior regions of both cerebral hemispheres, affecting mostly the occipital and parietal lobes.”  
4. Demyelinating disorders were considered given white-matter lesions but were excluded by the acute onset, symmetry, and posterior localization of the hyperintensities — “Typical MRI findings in PRES are of bilateral white-matter abnormalities in vascular watershed areas in the posterior regions of both cerebral hemispheres, affecting mostly the occipital and parietal lobes.”  
5. Vasculitis was considered because of potential small-vessel involvement but was excluded by the lack of vessel irregularities and by the classic imaging pattern of vasogenic edema — “Typical MRI findings in PRES are of bilateral white-matter abnormalities in vascular watershed areas in the posterior regions of both cerebral hemispheres, affecting mostly the occipital and parietal lobes.”  
6. Encephalitis was considered in light of headache and seizures but was excluded by normal inflammatory markers, absence of CSF findings, and the symmetrical posterior white-matter lesions on MRI — “Typical MRI findings in PRES are of bilateral white-matter abnormalities in vascular watershed areas in the posterior regions of both cerebral hemispheres, affecting mostly the occipital and parietal lobes.”
